Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 19, to amend the Exchequer Court Act. He said: The purpose of this Bill is to provide that, in cases of appeals from the decision of the Commissioner of Patents, in which case the Commissioner is entitled to appeal and to defend his decision, there shall be on the part of the Commisioner a right to appeal to the Supreme Court. There is presently on the part of the other party a right to appeal to the Supreme Court, and as the Commissioner figures in the proceedings as a representative of the public interest, it seemed only right that he should have the same right of appeal that the private party has.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs

No date has yet been fixed for the next Imperial Conference and there is no intention that it shall be held this year. It is anticipated, however, that a meeting of the Prime Ministers of the different parts of the Empire will be held in June next.
2.	The agenda for this meeting of Prime Ministers has not yet been settled, but it is expected that among the subjects for discussion will be the question of the renewal of the Treaty of Alliance with Japan of the thirteenth July, 1911, and the question of naval policy based upon the principle of co-operation; while there will doubtless be a review and consultation upon the general course of the foreign policy of the Empire.
3.	Correspondence is proceeding upon the subject for discussion at the June meeting of Prime Ministers.
4. Necessarily any proposals resulting from the conference and affecting Canada must be subject to the approval of the Canadian Parliament.

In view of the quarantine measures placed upon certain ports in the United States with regard to immigrants arriving thereat, and in view of the fact that a large number of infected immigrants are arriving in the United States, have any precautions been taken by the Dominion of Canada to prevent these immigrants from being diverted to Canadian ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is true that
typhus cases have arrived at New York and the Federal Health Service of the United States have established rigid quarantine measures to prevent this disease entering the United States Any immigrants allowed to land in the United States will have passed so effective a cordon as to be assuredly free from danger and may safely be accepted by us should they cross our border.
The department, in anticipation of possible danger of this kind, some three months ago, sent Dr. H. B. Jeffs of the Immigration Medical Staff, to New York to look into and familiarize himself with the American system and report on any possible avenues of danger to Canada. On his return to Canada Dr. Laurin of Quebec followed him to New York for the same pur-

pose, and Dr. G. E. Martineau, Superintendent at Gross Isle Quarantine Station, Quebec, is proceeding to New York in a few days to continue the observations.
Our own quarantine stations on the Atlantic coast, namely, at Halifax and St. John, have been warned and are on the alert for any possible source of danger.

His Majesty's Minister was further instructed, if a report of Dr. Burnham's arrest should be confirmed, to demand his immediate release.

2. The charges of harsh treatment as received in the Department were couched in general terms indicating rather friction with the local authorities during a period of disturbed conditions due to war with

maintopic: OIL IN THE PRAIRIE PROVINCES. MR. GRIESBACH MOVES A RESODUTION WITH RESPECT TO OWNERS OF SURFACE RIGHTS.

speakeroldname: Mr. WILLIAM ANTROBUS GRIESBACH (West Edmonton) moved:
maintopic: OIL IN THE PRAIRIE PROVINCES. MR. GRIESBACH MOVES A RESODUTION WITH RESPECT TO OWNERS OF SURFACE RIGHTS.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, should oil be found and produced in or under any lands in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, in which ownership to the sub-surface is in the Crown, the owner of the surface right shall be entitled to one-sixteenth ct such oil, provided that such owner shall have made a homestead entry, or other entry, for the^ said land prior to the date of the application for the oil lease in the sub-surface. And whereas, all existing leases contain a provision that they are subject to the provisions of the regulations in force at the time of the granting of the same and also any regulations subsequently adopted. Therefore alteration should he made in the regulations to give the owner of the surface rights a similar interest in the oil produced under leases heretofore granted in which no development work has been done upon the said lands under the said leases.
He said: The House may not be aware that a somewhat different system of land tenure prevails in the prairie provinces from that which obtains in the other parts of Canada. My information is that in the remaining provinces of Canada the old common law title exists, that is to say that the owner owns from the centre of the earth to the sky. That was the situation in the prairie provinces prior to October 31, 1887. Up to that time the Crown grant gave a title from the centre of the

earth to the sky, and the owner of the land owned all that there was to own. On the 31st October, 1887, the Crown began the policy of granting titles to the surface rights only, and reserving to the Grown the ownership in all mines and minerals which might underly the surface. During the past two or three years there has been much information to suggest that oil in large quantities would be discovered in the prairie provinces. During the last six months the evidence has accumulated to such an extent that it may now be reasonably assumed that the oil resources of Western Canada will prove to be in tremendous volume and ultimately of tremendous value to the Dominion. The State is interested, and this House is interested, having regard for this discovery and for its "potential value. The House is interested in seeing that the State shall be safeguarded in this great discovery. It ought likewise to be interested in seeing that those persons more nearly and more directly concerned are equally protected in this great discovery. The situation now is that the Crown owns the oil and the landowner owns the surface, and the titles that exist in Western Canada are largely, if not almost entirely, of this class. It is true that the railway companies and the Hudson's Bay Company hold their land grants under the old common law title without reservation, but the vast bulk of land titles in Western Canada are as I have described. If oil is discovered, the Crown may upon application issue oil leases to any persons who apply in respect to lands which are owned by hundreds of thousands of homesteaders throughout the Prairie Provinces. It is quite true that the owner of the surface rights may himself apply for an oil lease, but whatever the theory may be, and whatever the policy of the law may be-and the policy is that all men shall be equal before the law-the actual fact is that the real owner of land in the western provinces, the homesteader, the farmer, the pioneer, is completely out of touch with this oil development. The man who files is the capitalist, the investor, the speculator, the man who has access to many newspapers and scientific works and who is in touch with geologists and other technical experts. The result is that the farmer, the homesteader, the pioneer, who has developed the country, who is paying taxes to build roads and bridges, and who has made it possible for people to come 371
in and exploit the country will find that some day the Government has given a lease to drill for oil upon his property, and should oil be discovered he has to sit by with his hands folded while the oil lessee walks off with all the profits there may be in that discovery.
In the United States, where the old common law titles prevails, and where the owner of the surface owns the subsurface as well, the practice has grown up and has almost come to have the force of law, that if the owner leases his land for oil drilling purposes it is on terms that he shall receive one-eighth of the oil discovered. So that the owner of land throughout the United States almost entirely should oil be discovered on his property, is sure to receive one-eighth of all the oil discovered should he so provide in his lease.
In the western country the regulations provide that an oil lease may be granted without the knowledge of the owner of the land. True, the owner of the surface rights is entitled to be indemnified for any damage that may be done to his holding, but that is all he gets out of it. Any person can apply for an oil lease upon oil being discovered; pays a royalty of five per cent, subsequently rising to ten per cent on the oil which may be gained.
I propose by this resolution that while the interests of the state are safeguarded, and the state may continue to receive the-revenues which it has legislated that it shall receive, nevertheless the owner of the land-who in our case is the farmer, the homesteader, the pioneer, the man who has made settlement and development possible, without which development it would be absolutely impossible for drilling machinery to be taken into the country-shall participate in the benefit accruing from the discovery of oil on his property, to the extent of one-sixteenth of the oil gained.
I pointed out a moment ago that in the United States the land owner is entitled by custom and as a matter of his own contract to receive one-eighth of the oil. Here I allow one-sixteenth, for two reasons. First in this country the owner does not own the subsurface rights, which remain in the Crown, and for which the Crown claims a royalty. Under my proposal the man who drills for oil under a lease from the Government would be required to pay to the owner of the land one-sixteenth of the oil gained and to the Crown five per cent, rising to ten per cent. If you equalise the royalty and the percentage, you will find

that on the basis of a royalty of one-eighth the equivalent is 121 per cent, and that five per cent is equal to one-twentieth.
If the House agrees to this proposal and allows the owner to receive one-sixteenth for the oil taken under his property, which is equal to 68 per cent, the man who has the oil lease will have to pay the 61 per cent to the owner of the land and five per cent to the Government, or 118 per cent; whereas were he to make his private arrangement with the owner of the land in the United States the oil lease would have to pay 121 per cent. Therefore my proposal so far as the oil driller is concerned is better than the arrangement that exists in the oil fields of the United States. And the advantage is this, that whereas under our system of titles ownership of the subsurface rights is in the Crown we have growing out of this discovery the possibility of the state participating in the value [DOT]of the discovery, and we have at the same time given to the surface owner the opportunity of participating in the oil discovery.
I attach great importance to this matter, and I think the time to deal with it is now, instead of waiting until the whole country is upset with excitement should big oil discoveries take place. I venture to say that if the matter is not dealt with until then, and drilling begins everywhere, followed by oil discoveries in many places, the people of the.West will wake up to the fact that they have had this great wealth under their feet and that now the full benefit is being reaped by those coming in from the outside and who have not borne the heat and burden of the day incident to pioneering in the West.
It may be that I should continue to read the resolution further to show how no principle of equity or justice is violated by the proposal. I go on to state:
-provided that such owner shall have made a homestead entry, or other, for the said land prior to the date of the application for the oil lease in the subsurface.
In the case of vacant land where an applicant for an oil lease has made application prior to any homestead right being granted, then the man who subsequently took the homestead would be doing so with his eyes open and would have no grievance. I provide that where the homesteader has his entry first, and somebody files an oil lease subsequently, then the discoverer of oil shall pay one-sixteenth per cent.
It is desirable, since the country is largely plastered at this moment with oil leases, that some attempt be made to deal with the
]Mr. Griesbach. [
situation where a homesteader has his homestead filed upon by the holder of an oil lease. The provision I would make in that respect is this: that the power which the Government have to alter these oil regulations from time to time-a power which they do exercise when they feel like it-be used to provide that the royalty of one-sixteenth of the owners shall be made effective in cases where, notwithstanding the fact that a lease has been issued, no development work has been done by the leaseholder. In cases where the leaseholder has done development work it might not be fair to interfere with the terms of his lease, but where he has done no development work under his lease his position is precisely the same, to all intents and purposes, as it would have been before he made his application, and in that case the regulations should be altered as I have suggested.
In this eastern country, from which the majority of the members of the House come, this may appear to be a very small matter, and my action on it might seem to be premature. It may occur to hon. members that as oil is not actually being produced there is no reason why the House should busy itself with a matter of this kind in anticipation of the production. But I believe it would be wisdom on the part of this House to deal with the matter now; to deal with it before a greater number of applications for oil leases are filed and before the people of the prairie provinces wake up to the fact that this great wealth which they believe to be theirs really belongs to somebody else; that the benefit and advantage of the discovery and the tremendous profits that accrue commence to go elsewhere, there will be grave dissatisfaction and grave unrest,
4 p.m. and ultimately the matter will have to be dealt with.
I do not propose to raise in this connection the question of the ownership of the natural resources of the West-a question which might properly be discussed under this head. But I do think that now is the time to go into this matter and to introduce such legislation as will ensure to the state its just and fair participation in the valuable discoveries that are about to be made, and at the same time to ensure fair and reasonable participation also to the private individual, the farmer, the homesteader, the pioneer of these western countries, to whose efforts are attributable the development of this vast and immensely valuable discovery.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: OIL IN THE PRAIRIE PROVINCES. MR. GRIESBACH MOVES A RESODUTION WITH RESPECT TO OWNERS OF SURFACE RIGHTS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this motion, had it been moved a year ago, would have been under the department over which I then presided. Now it is under the department of the hon. leader of the Senate, but I am more or less familiar with the history of oil regulations so far as the Dominion Government has control of oil, and I will endeavor to state to the House some considerations which bear upon the desire of the hon. member as expressed in this resolution.
The history of oil production in Canada has shown as yet a very meagre total output. I am not sure that my percentages are right-the hon. member for Lambton would be familiar with the figures-but I think that we in Canada as yet produce only about two per cent of the oil consumed in this country; consequently the record to date is rather a record of search and exploitation-of hope deferred, rather than hope fulfilled. So much has this been the case that for many years, in place of seeking to obtain a revenue by royalty from oil production, the Government of Canada has placed a premium upon oil production, and very considerable sums have, over a period of many years, gone from the treasury as a bonus on the production of oil in this country. Indeed, I question whether the oil industry of Ontario would have survived in any substantial degree had such a system of bonus not prevailed. There have of late years been very hopeful indications of oil discovery on a large scale in Western Canada. There has, of course, been oil production there already, but the record of the whole mater so far as the West is concerned up to date is rather a record of rentals paid and the administration of leases sold by speculators than a record of actual oil production by men who seriously intended to produce. The treasury has come off much better than the investor in relation to oil in Western Canada up to now. While it was the case that a bonus was being paid to encourage oil exploration and oil production about twelve years ago, it was deemed expedient by the then Government that this degree of encouragement should be given: that leases might issue up to 1931, which would contain a clause exempting the lessee from all royalty whatsoever. Many leases of that character were issued. About a year and a half ago that regulation was rescinded, as it then appeared that there might at any time be oil discoveries on a large scale. Not only was that regulation rescinded, but efforts were made to ascertain what leases were in arrears to such a degree as would justify cancellation, in order that as many as possible of the dead leases outstanding under the old regulations could be made to lapse, and provision was made that at any time thereafter oil royalties might be imposed. After I ceased to hold that office, the present Minister of the Interior introduced regulations, which were adopted, providing that in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta a royalty should be imposed grading upwards from 21 to 10 per cent on leases thereafter issued and on leases issued since the date when the old regulations were rescinded, and it was possible to impose royalties on oils found under those leases. Such are the regulations today in relation to the three provinces, the royalty grading from 21 to 10 per cent,
I think the 21 per cent being for five years, the 5 per cent for a little longer period, and the 10 per cent after that, and an entrant may enter for 1920 acres of land and obtain a lease therefor.
The prospect of oil appears, however, to be mostly in territory north of the three provinces, and some weeks ago regulations as to the Northwest Territories were put into effect, those regulations being of a character radically different from any yet imposed in Canada. They provided that the explorer or prospector may take out a permit for four sections; but until there is oil production, this is a permit and nothing more. He may get a lease upon actually discovering oil, but he can get a lease only for one section out of the four, the other three reverting then and there to the Crown. He thus becomes entitled to a lease for 640 acres only, and he becomes liable to a royalty of from 5 to 10 per cent, that is to say, 5 per cent until 1st April, 1926, and thereafter 10 per cent. The regulations comprise a series of 22 pages, but those are, broadly speaking, their outstanding features.
My hon. friend's proposal is to impose on all lessees who take out leases hereafter, as well upon those who have leases which make them subject to regulations imposed subsequent to the issue of the lease, the obligation of contributing one-sixteenth of the output to the owner of the surface rights, in cases where the Crown is the owner of only the sub-surface and where the surface itself is held by a homestead entrant who entered prior to the taking out of the lease, or where it is

maintopic: DESTRUCTION OF DOCUMENTS AT PRINTING BUREAU

speechtext:
Hon, RODOLPHE LEMIEUX moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, a drastic investigation should be held in connection

with the wanton destruction of most valuable documents alleged to have taken place during recess at the Printing Bureau.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to delay the House with this motion. It was drafted merely to call the attention of the House and the Government to the very serious-accident, shall I say-which took place a few months ago at the Printing Bureau. From the press reports it appears that several tons of most valuable documents were destroyed. I understand that a firm was appointed by the Government not very long ago to investigate various departments, and especially the Printing Bureau, and we were informed by the press-I do not know whether it is a fact, but such was the report-that whilst this firm was proceeding with its investigation many very valuable documents which had accumulated in the Government buildings since Confederation, and even prior to that, were ordered to he destroyed. I remember reading in the papers at the time of this destruction, that some of the blue books which were destroyed or sold would have been most valuable to the public archives of Canada; in fact, one of the archivists told me that some of these documents could not be found elsewhere in the world to-day, and their value could not be estimated in terms of dollars and cents. I am told that on different occasions from different countries of the world, especially from Great Britain, requests have come for some of these documents, which dated very far back in the history of the Confederation. Now the object of my motion is	to	ascertain who	was
responsible for this destruction, what documents have been destroyed, and whether the Government intends to make a drastic investigation so that punishment will be meted out to the parties who are found to be responsible. I cannot for one moment believe that the gentlemen who were engaged in the investigation of the Printing Bureau were authorized by anyone in the Government to destroy these documents. Blue books are published from year to year, and sometimes a great many of them remain on the shelves; they may not be wanted presently, but they may be wanted later on, and we must always provide for future needs. I remember reading the history of the Parliament Buildings' fire in Montreal in 1849. The story of that fire, which occurred under circumstances with which we are all familiar, was told by a gentleman who occupies a very enviable position in the world of letters, and he gives a list of the public documents and blue books which were destroyed and cannot be found anywhere else in the libraries of Canada. What a national loss such a fire was for the writers on the history of Canada! With regard to the destruction that has taken place recently, an archivist in the employ of the Government told me that to his own personal knowledge some of the blue books which have disappeared were invaluable and could not be replaced.
I shall not delay the House further, but I should like to know from the right hon. the Prime Minister if an investigation is being held, and if so, the nature of that investigation, and whether the Government intends to take the necessary steps to punish the guilty parties?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DESTRUCTION OF DOCUMENTS AT PRINTING BUREAU
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) is also referred to in one, if not more, questions that appear on the Order Paper to-day. The first time this matter came to my attention, speaking from memory, was about four months ago, perhaps only three. I made such inquiry as I was able to make of other members of the Government and elsewhere. The complaints that were raised were very much of the same nature as those expressed to-day by the hon. member to the effect that valuable books had been destroyed, or rather, it seems to me the way it was put was this-that they had been turned over to the contractor who had the contract for the waste paper that gathers around the Parliament Buildings. Valuable documents that had been stowed away were, either by mistake or design, turned over to him. I think that is the way it was put to me. At all events, these documents had been put out of the road and were no longer the property of the Government. I am glad to be able to say to the hon member that the Government took action in this matter some time ago. I cannot recall the exact date, but it must be now a matter of some months. The inquiry was ordered under the Inquiries' Act, and his Honour, Judge Snider, of the County Court of Wentworth, was appointed a Commissioner under that Act with the fullest possible powers, because the Act itself gives the powers. The wording of the Order in Council was in the amplest language, to investigate and ascertain who was responsible for the destruction and removal of these books and documents.

There has been no report from that commission as yet. I know they have held sittings, but I do not know whether they have concluded their investigation. The Government requested Col. O. M. Biggar to act as Government Counsel on the enquiry to assist Judge Snider in the investigation. The House will remeher that under the terms of the Dominion Elections Act which passed last session Col. Biggar was appointed Chief Electoral Officer, and to him was also assigned the duty of assisting as Counsel for the Government in investigations of this character. Consequently he was the appropriate Counsel to select in this instance, and I know that he has been engaged with Judge Snider in the investigation. I made enquiries a moment ago of the Minister of Justice to ascertain whether he had any word as to reports from the investigation, and he tells me he has not. I am therefore of opinion that His Honour Judge Snider has not yet reported, but I can assure the hon. member that I am awaiting the report with interest, and if it shows that there are parties guilty of crime in any degree they ought to be punished, and it is the intention of the Government not to refrain from proceeding with their punishment.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.

speechtext:
Mr. ANDREW ROSS McMASTER (Brome) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10 to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, the atmosphere of the Chamber this afternoon lends itself to the observations which I have to bring before the House, as the matter is of an essentially non-partisan and, I trust, of a non-contentious character. The atmosphere, the member for An-tigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) suggests sub-rosa, is of a chilly nature and certainly the Speaker or the Deputy-Speaker might endeavour to prevent the draughts which circulate in the Chamber from affecting members from time to time. However, that is not the subject of my remarks this afternoon. The object of this Bill is to make it incumbent upon ministers of the Crown to resign all directorships which they hold in incorporated companies when they accept their portfolios. The first argument I wish to make in favour of the principle of the Bill is that it is in consonance with the best Canadian practice. My information is, Mr. Speaker, that when the member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) the former Premier, accepted office in 1911 he resigned all directorships which he held, and encouraged all his colleagues to do so. Had that wholesome practice been followed, there would have been no necessity for the debate which is going to take place this afternoon.
My next point, Mr. Speaker, is that the abandonment of directorships by ministers of the Crown is in line with the best British practice. It is not always the case in Great Britain that men who occupy the positions of ministers of the Crown resign their directorships, but my opinion is, and I believe it is correct, that it is the best British practice to resign directorships when accepting a portfolio. I read from the British Hansard, Fourth Series, Vol. 93, Page 216, a citation which I take from a discussion of a similar character to the one we are now entering upon, held in the British House some years ago. The precedent of Lord Rathmore had been alluded to. He was a very honourable man, but his case

formed a very bad precedent for his was a most striking case of a minister of the Crown uniting with that position the. directorship of innumerable companies. According to the directory of directors that gentleman was a director in no less than ten companies. Now, I think that at least the ministers of the Crown will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, when I lay down as one of the premises of my argument that the life of a minister of the Crown in this country is one of arduous and unremitting toil.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: La Banque d'Hochelaga.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, La Banque
d'Hochelaga, La Banque Provinciale-in my hypothetical case we will give the province of Quebec and the French institutions full and ample representation. Now, suppose at the same time the Minister of Finance-and this is a hypothetical proposition, absurd on its face-was a director of the Bank of Montreal, and suppose he gave this position to the Bank of Montreal, what an outcry there would be, and how the people would think that something was wrong. How easily the public would think he had been influenced in making his choice by the fact that he was a director of that bank. Those are merely hypothetical illustrations, but I say they show the advisability of making it impossible for such things to happen by providing that when ministers of the Crown accept office they should cease being directors of companies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are the possible objections to my proposal? They are, I imagine, certain possible objections. It may be said that laying down the proposition as I have done in the Bill which I have introduced I have been too wide and sweeping. We can imagine a case of this sort, a minister of the Crown being a director of a mutual life insurance company. Such a company is of a quasi-benevolent nature. I suppose there is no truer philanthropy that a man of moderate means can practice than to insure his life for the benefit of his wife and children. It may be that our insurance laws are so carefully administered that loss in such a company is practically impossible, and that the minister in giving the influence of his name to a mutual life insurance company is merely encouraging people to do what is right. The same sort of argument might apply in large measure to a director of a savings bank. I can quite imagine that hon. members may bring to the consideration of this question arguments which may tend to show that the proposal is too wide. Why have I brought it in this wide form? Because I believe that if you try to draw the line you will meet with more trouble than if you do not admit the wisdom

of directorships of any sort or kind being held by ministers of the Crown. Suppose a man has built up a business and subsequently turns it into a one-man company. It may be said: Well, it is unfair to ask that man to give up the directorship of that company if he joins the Government. There may be something in that, but the answer I would make to this: that if he is going to do his duty as a minister of the Crown he really will not have time to attend to his business.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question here?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Would the hon. member carry it this step further: that if a man was engaged in business-had not formed his one-man company, but was in a firm or was carrying on business-he should abandon or liquidate his business upon becoming a member of the Government?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
No, I would not say that. I grant, Mr. Speaker, that the line is pretty narrow. It is much the same as in the case of the age at which a person may legally make a contract; if a man is twenty-one years of age he may legally make a contract, but if he is twenty years and nine months of age any contract he makes might be subject to attack. I admit that the distinction is pretty fine, but I do not propose to go so far. I do not think it would be in the public interest to say that a man should give up all his private business when he becomes a Minister of the Crown. I do think that if he can so arrange matters that he will be able to give up all active participation in his private business, leaving it to others, and to devote his whole time and attention to the public business, that is the ideal thing for him to do. After all, Mr. Speaker

we are discussing this matter in the most friendly fashion-how much practice of the law can the Prime Minister carry on at present at Portage La Prairie? Not very much; he has had to give it up, and there are members on this side who, if they went into the Cabinet, would have to lay aside their law practice for the time being.
And the man who lays aside his law business is not merely giving up, so to speak, the interest on his capital; he is jeopardizing even his capital and is jeopardizing his practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Of course, somewhat more is expected of lawyers than of other classes of the community.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: There is a great deal in that. I do not know any class of the community which renders more unselfish public service than the lawyers do. The doctors, too, give a great deal of unselfish public service, and perhaps more unselfish private service than the lawyers do.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Why has the hon. gentleman set a period of fifteen days as the limit of time within which a man must resign his directorship after becoming sworn in as a Minister of the Crown? I should think it would be better to provide a period of fifteen days after his election, because it might so happen that after the election there would be no occasion for his resigning any directorship.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
That is a matter
which, I think could be taken up in committee. As the father of the Bill, I would be prepared to accept an amendment in that connection.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: To be a director in a concern a man has necessarily to be a shareholder. Must a Minister, in resigning his directorship, also part with his shares?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: No, I do not propose that for a moment.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Then his interest is there just the same.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
His interest is there, it is quite true. But a shareholder has not. as a rule, the same control of policy that a director has. Quite often in large companies a man is asked to subscribe to shares, or is sometimes given qualifying shares, so that the company may enjoy either the direct benefit of his experience and business ability, or the
5 p.m. prestige of his name.
I frankly grant that you may ask me questions which are difficult to answer as regards the differentiation of private interests as between the shareholder and the director. I can imagine a case in which the private interest of a large shareholder in a company is much greater than the private interest of a director would be who might be a small shareholder. We could not, in fairness, shut out people who were shareholders in all companies from membership in the Government, because if we did we should too greatly limit the choice.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Suppose a man holds twenty-five per cent of the stock of some institution, and is a director and prominent member of it. He enters the Government, he resigns his directorship and retains his

stock in the company. All he does is simply hide from the public his active interest, still retaining his real interest in the company. What is the difference?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Well, there is this difference: It is true that he retains his personal interest, but his fiduciary interest disappears. My hon. friend will realize that an honourable man will be more careful of the interests which he represents as a trustee than he will be of his own interests, and the cutting off of directors from portfolios does cut off from the Cabinet the possibility of conflicting fiduciary interests-the fiduciary interests of the director who represents his shareholders and that of the Minister of the Crown who represents the whole people. I quite agree that the personal interest of the shareholder remains; that is something which I do not think we can get rid of without unduly limiting the choice of Ministers of the Crown. But it is quite possible to prevent the carrying of interlocking directorates- which, I think, are now far too prevalent throughout the country-into the circle of the Cabinet itself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Does the hon. member not think that if his Bill is to be accepted it should, under our present practice, apply as well to the leader of the Opposition?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: I would have not the slightest objection to its applying to the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: And to the leaders of both Oppositions?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: I know my own leader and can speak for him; I am sure he would not have the slightest objection to having it apply to him. As regards the leader of the Opposition sitting angularly opposite, I cannot speak for him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: But does the principle apply?	.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: There is, of course, the consideration, as the member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) remarks, that there is no salary attached to the position of the leader of the other Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: That is not the point.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
That is not the great point, I admit. If that is the only thing standing in the way of the Government's acceptance of my Bill, I would be willing
to go one step further and have it apply to the leader of the Opposition as well.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: It would be of no use to have the one without the other.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Perhaps I
should say right at the moment that I should feel it distinctly in the public interest to have the provision apply to the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: I really had not my hon. friend in mind; I was just leading through him to the other.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
A sort of oratio
obliqua. In bringing my remarks to a close,
I must thank the House for the kindly, friendly and patient attention that has been, given to my remarks. I am asking only that we place upon the Statute Book what I regard to be the best and the prevailing practice. I do not believe the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen), who leads the Government to-day, is a director in a company. He indicates by a shake of the head that he is not. I know that the last leader of the Government, the present member for King's N.S. (Sir Robert Borden), resigned his directorships. I remember, shortly after he became Prime Minister, having to examine the books of a very small company down in Nova Scotia and seeing on the books that he had sent in his resignation because he had become a minister of the Crown. I know that the only directorship which my late leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, ever accepted, was in a mutual life insurance company. Therefore, I am asking this Government to accept legislation that will merely crystallize in the form of a statute the best prevailing practice. It may be said, of course, and it will be urged, perhaps in this debate, that we should leave this matter to the individual feeling of delicacy and propriety of the ministers themselves. That has not been done in regard to senators and members. Under the Senate and House of Commons Act, their obligation to refrain from bringing before the House legislation in which they are interested, as lawyers, for instance, is very clearly set forth, and their in*-ability to have an interest in a contract with the Government is also very clearly set forth. Therefore, that argument is offset by the fact that we have crystallized in the form of a statute the best prevailing practice as to members of Parliament, and I submit that what I ask for is right, and that it is calculated to enhance the honour and prestige of public men in this Dominion of Canada.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext: He would not be disqualified; if he accepted the portfolio, he would have to resign his directorship. His directorship would not prevent his being chosen; but after he was chosen, he would have to choose between the retention of his portfolio and the retention of his directorship.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
I quite understand that, but that, to my mind, is rather a technical argument. A man publicly has his name on his letter head or bill head or

whatever you like as a director of the company in which he is interested; he then becomes a member of a government, and he removes his name as director, and if he is asked across the floor of this House, if he is a director of this company, he says: "No," but practically his position is the same as it was before; he does not sell out; he cannot dispossess himself; he cannot sacrifice his rights; it is not likely that he would sacrifice his rights, and yet he may be in a position to be of great service to the government of whatever party it may be. My hon. friend probably did not have that matter which I have outlined as much in mind as he had what he termed interlocking directorates. If you stand several individuals up in line, all of them in different occupations and professions, how is it possible to say who is best qualified for Cabinet rank? A man might be a director in one or two or more financial corporations-let us get away from the smaller businesses- a government might be formed, and his services, because of his wider experience in the affairs of this country might be thought to be better than those of another man whose name is not connected with any corporation. The men whose names appear as directors of corporations are generally understood to be men who understand the affairs of this country as well as and, in most cases, have wider experiences in our country's affairs than other men, and consequently they would be more useful to this country. I cannot, therefore, see how you can pass a law to debar such men from becoming members of government in this country any more than you can pass a law saying who shall be members of government, and what occupations they shall hold in order to be members. My hon. friend gave some precedents in England, but the situation there is very different from what it is in Canada. Ninety per cent of the members of this House, whether they are in professions or in business, have risen from the ranks, and everybody, if he is looked upon generally in the community in which he resides, as a man of sufficient experience to become a member of a government, is supposed to be qualified in one sense or another for such a position. As I said when I rose, I did not intend to say more than a few words on this question, and I have not covered the subject at all; but it seems to me, notwithstanding the fact that the hon. member for Brome has approached the subject in what appears to be a very impartial way, his argument is full of inconsistencies.

Mr. JOHN H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough) : Mr. Speaker, I was struck with the speech of the hon. member for Toronto East (Sir Edward Kemp), but I think he has forgotten the fact that Parliament has already taken the step that he thinks is a hardship. Parliament has provided that a member of this House must not do any business with the Government. We have gone so far as to debar every member of the House of Commons in this respect. If my hon. friend will refer to the provisions of Chapter 10, cf the Revised Statutes, he will see that the most drastic provision to this, effect is made. My hon. friend's illustration of John Smith in his personal capacity, and John Smith Limited, does not apply, because even now if John Smith is not Limited he cannot be a minister and do business with the Government. He cannot be a member of this House and do business with the Government.
My hon. friend points out how difficult it would be to find a man to accept a position as minister of the Crown if he was prohibited from engaging in business. But we prohibit them already, because if John Smith is in business and becomes a member of this House, or a minister of the Crown, in his personal capacity he must not do any business with the Government. If he does, he becomes disqualified as a member of the House and as a minister of the Crown. So we have that prohibition already. Why should we make any distinction between John Smith in his personal capacity and . John Smith Limited? Why should we prohibit John Smith in his personal capacity from doing business with the Government, if we are not at the same time going to prohibit him as John Smith Limited? The same principle is involved in both cases. If my hon. friend is not willing to pass this Bill, I think he ought to be willing to repeal Chapter 10, of the Revised Statutes, which provides that John Smith must not do any business with the Government. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal of my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Me-Master) is sound. Shareholders are excepted under the law because, of course, it would be a hardship for a man of any means to have to dispose of his shares; that would be throwing away his property. But a director is in a much different position. My hon. friend from Brome has pointed out very clearly that it is the
duty of a director acting in a fiduciary capacity to try and get a contract from the Government for his firm; it is his duty to do everything he can to make money for the shareholders that he represents. On the other hand, it is his duty as a minister of the Crown probably to give the contract to somebody else. These are two conflicting duties, and I can see no great hardship in compelling a man who accepts a position as minister of the Crown to resign his directorship in any company he is interested in. My hon. friend from Brome has pointed out that that is the practice already with some members of this Government. Very recently my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCurdy) after joining the Government resigned his position in the firm in Nova Scotia with which he was formerly connected. Similar instances have been pointed out by my hon. friend from Brome. The practice exists now. I think it is a good practice, and that it would be a good thing to have it embodied in the statutes.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed
this debate with very great interest, and with my hon. friend from Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp) I commend the tone adopted by my good friend from Brome (Mr. Me-Master) in discussing this important question. While I have not gone deeply into the matter, I must say that I differ from my hon. friend from Toronto in the view which he takes of this Bill. He says that v men ought not to be debarred from joining the Government by the fact that they have large interests in limited companies and are directors on their boards. My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) has just cited the section of the Revised Statutes which debars members of parliament from entering into any contracts with the Government. But there is a more glaring instance. My hon. friend will also find that the Revised Statutes of Canada provide for the independence of the Bench. Some years ago this Parliament amended the Judicature Act to provide that judges who had been appointed directors and were drawing directors' fees in joint stock companies or in any other company must resign. I may be told at once that no judge was ever accused of being partial in his decisions because he was a director of a company. That may be the case, but there is a great principle involved in this matter, and it is that the public must

have absolute confidence in the integrity and probity of those who administer the law. It was for that purpose-that the public might respect the more the Bench of Canada-that this Parliament decided that judges should not be directors of any company. The legislation evoked considerable discussion at the time, and some of the judges protested against what they called this hardship being imposed upon them; yet public opinion ratified the action of Parliament. Every litigant approved of it because, as we say in common parlance, Caesar's wife must be above suspicion. Justice must be protected not only by herself-and I use the word "herself" because I see her living on the Bench, personified by the judge who administers the law- she must also be protected against her own self, and that is the reason why Parliament decided that judges should have no interests as directors of companies. I may be told that ministers of the Crown are not judges. True, in a sense; but they make the laws. They decide long before-hand what laws shall be introduced, and therefore it seems to me they have an equal, if not a greater responsibility than the judges themselves.
I might give another illustration to show how sensitive public opinion is in regard to those who administer the law. My right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) knows that in our province -I do not know whether the same plan has been adopted in other provinces- the relative of a judge to the second degree is debarred from pleading before the judge, nor can any member of his firm appear before him. So intent is public opinion that justice shall be above suspicion. I commend again my hon. friend from Brome for his remarks this afternoon. This is a matter that applies to both parties, to ministers of the Crown of to-day, and to ministers of the Crown of tomorrow. It is in their interests that they should be protected against their own weaknesses; for we are all human. Public opinion should be saisfied tha^ they have no monetary interest which might conflict with their duty as ministers of the Crown.
I may be told, as stated by my hon. friend from Toronto a moment ago, that business men of great ability and of substance might be debarred from giving their country the benefit of their experience. Well, let me recall to my hon. friend first of all the fact that the salaries of the ministers of the Crown have been increased. But I put that aside and I say is not the honour of being a minister of the

Crown, the honour of being sworn in as a Privy Councillor, a reward by itself? In my humble judgment, no man should hesitate, when accepting that honour, to put aside his private interests. I think I am right in this, Mr. Speaker. I am glad to say that never since Confederation, up to the present time, has there been any reason on the part of the public to suspect the personal integrity of the Prime Ministers of Canada, and I include with pleasure in this statement the name of the right hon. gentleman who to-day as Prime Minister presides over the destinies of this country. But I say that it is in the interests of the ministers of the Crown, and of good government and of the good reputation of Parliament, that public opinion should be satisfied that there are no conflicting interests between ministers as such and any directors of private (concerns. Why, it is obvious that any day of the month a minister of the Crown who has charge of a large spending department- let us take, for example, the Public Works Department, the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or the Department of the Interior might be put in a very awkward position as between his fiduciary interests as member of a board and his public duties on the other hand. It may happen any day, and therefore I think, without having gone very deeply into the matter, that my hon. friend is living up to British custom, to precedent, and tradition in advocating this legislation. My hon. friend from Toronto spoke of the difference that existed between public men in this country and public men in the Old Country. Let me tell him that in the Old Country of late there has been a hue and cry in the public press and elsewhere against members of the House of Lords, ministers of the Crown-and that is not done very often with ministers of the Crown -lending their names as promoters or directors of boards. Mr. Speaker, if I were not afraid of hurting the feelings of any one, I could mention the name of a gentleman I have in mind who played a very great part in the history of the British Empire, a name which brought to his family and to his country much honour and glory. And yet that name was besmirched. Why? Because in a moment of weakness the bearer of that great name allowed it to figure in a promoters' scheme. I think of that name because it is so very eminent. But there are dozens and dozens of such names which have been lent to satisfy some promoter's greed. Now, do

you believe that it is making for the honour and respect of public life that such things should be? I should like to have this discussion go a little further so that we might hear both sides of the question. It strikes me, after having heard my hon. friend and the objections that were made by some of the hon. gentlemen on the other side-mild objections I must say-that this is a needed reform and one which is consistent with British traditions.

speakeroldname: Mr. FRANCIS HENRY KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora) :
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
The manner in
which this discussion has been carried on shows clearly that there is no ulterior motive behind it. But I think that the hon. gentlemen who have been advocating this proposal have not given to it the fullest consideration which its ramifications warrant. I cannot see why a minister of the Crown should be compelled to resign his directorship in any company, whether they might or might not have anything to do with government business or with Parliament, unless you carry the principle to every member of Parliament. I would not object at all if it were laid down as public law that no member of Parliament should be a director in any company, if that were deemed advisable. Personally, I think it inadvisable, because there are thousands of companies that have no transactions with any of the offices of government. But to say that no Cabinet Minister should be permitted to hold any directorship in any corporation is going too far, unless you apply the principle also to members of Parliament. The public are well protected to-day by the independence of Parliament Act, Chapter 10. There it is laid down most specifically in Section 14 that no person, directly or indirectly, shall be allowed to have any interests in any contract or agreement, either through trustee or otherwise, if he is a member 'of Parliament.

Does the hon. member
think that that includes a member who is a director or has a controlling interest in an incorporated company?	'

speechtext: As I understand, it includes any person. The Act reads as follows:-

statute as at present.
Mr. KEEF.ER: Chapter ten?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Section 14 of chapter 10
says that no contract with the Government
is permitted if a person has any interest in it directly or indirectly. Then, section 18 says further that in every such contract there must be a clause providing that no member of Parliament is to have any share or interest in such contract, or commission, or benefit to be derived therefrom. Such is to-day expressly forbidden. There is a penalty and this qualification for any contravention of the statute. There is only one exception, you are allowed to be a shareholder. Now is it not the interest in the company as a shareholder, that should be in question? The attack is only made upon the principle of the minister of the Crown being a director. I think the Bill as drafted has not been carefully thought out. There are many things which might receive further consideration. Why should the Independence of Parliament Act be at all restricted and apply to only ministers of the Crown as directors when that Act strikes directly at every member of Parliament?
I see a great deal of force in what the member for Toronto said. If a man is carrying on a business as a partnership or as an individual, which might be a very large business, there is no interference. But if he finds it advisable to incorporate a company and to retain a seat on the board of directors in order to have some guidance of its affairs, why could he not as before incorporation, be a member of the government?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
I strongly approve the principles of the Bill presented by my hon. friend from Brome. The measure serves two purposes, one being to leave the minister free to devote his whole time to public business. I think that when a gentleman enters the Government of Canada he should be prepared to' devote his whole time and attention to the country's affairs. At the last session of Parliament the salaries of the ministers were increased so as to render them independent of their ordinary profession or calling, and to afford them a decent living. Another important purpose to be served by this Bill, which is perhaps more important, is to secure the independence of a minister so that his private interests or the interests of his friends, or of his company, should not conflict with the public interests. I would go further, and I would say that a minister should not invariably have to sell his interests in any company when he enters the Government. I would permit him to be a shareholder so long as his company did not do any business with the Government. But



the moment that company engaged upon any Government business the minister should be disqualified from remaining any longer as a shareholder in it. I would extend the principle of this Act to members of Parliament as my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) suggested. But I think my hon. friend misapprehends the meaning of section 10 of the Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons. Section 19 permits a shareholder in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement with the Government of Canada, except any company which undertakes a contract for the building of a public works. A few years ago I presented a Bill to this House to disqualify any member, or any Senator, from having a seat in Parliament if he were a director, or had a controlling interest, in any company doing business with the Government. During the war many companies, in which members of Parliament and senators were directors, or had a controlling interest, sold supplies to the Government. As my hon. friend from Toronto has said there is a great difference in the manner of carrying on business today compared with that of twenty-five or thirty years ago. To-day business is not so much done by individuals as by incorporated companies. At the time the Act was framed business was transacted mostly by individuals. The statute, as quoted by my hon. friend from Port Arthur, provides that no person directly or indirectly, or with any other, can do business with the Government, but it excepts any shareholder in an incorporated company. Well, I would not go so far as to disqualify a member of Parliament or a Senator who might be simply a shareholder in a company doing business with the Government. But I would disqualify a member of Parliament or a Senator who was a director, or had a controlling interest in a company which was doing business with the Government. If we want to preserve the independence of Parliament, and to have a Parliament independent of the Ministry, we should provide all the safeguards possible to secure that independence. When the Act was framed I believe such was the intention of its framers. But by reason of the fact that the method of doing business has been changed this independence is not fully secured, because incorporated companies in which members jf Parliament and members of the Senate have a controlling interest can do business with the Government. We know that some of these companies are one-man institutions 
or family organizations; strangers have only a few shares in them to qualify as directors. I think more wrong has been done by companies doing business with the Government than by particular individuals. I strongly endorse the principle of the Bill now before the House, but I would go further and exclude members of Parliament who are directors and have a controlling interest in incorporated companies doing business with the Government. Two years ago, when I presented a Bill to have the statute amended in this respect, I was met with the objection that some members of Parliament might be directors of printing companies who publish newspapers, and if their newspapers published Government advertisements they would be exposed to disqualification. In the Act respecting members of the Ontario legislature I believe there is a provision excepting members of the legislature who are shareholders or directors of companies publishing newspapers which in the ordinary course of business contain Government advertisements. I would be willing to incorporate that exception in the Federal statute. We have a provision similar to that in our Municipal Act to prevent the disqualification of members of the municipal council who, in the ordinary course of business, do any printing work for the municipality. I think with these exceptions the Act could be safely amended, and that we should amend it and secure fully the independence of ministers and of members of this House and of the Senate.

I should like to ask my hon. friend
from Brome (Mr. McMaster) if he is aware whether there is any English statute of similar character to the one he is introducing?	,

speechtext: No.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
I would have been surprised if he had found one because I recollect being in England when the late Lord Rhondda bought control of a nerve tonic called " Phosphozone," and although he was then a member of the British Government he promoted a company and put the specific on the market. He told how much good it had done his nerves and the nerves of others suffering from the effects of the war. That struck me as carrying things rather far. But I think it indicates that to-day there is no such statute in force in England as that now proposed by the hon. member for Brome. In this country we

Have had this Independence of Parliament legislation on the statute books, I suppose, for nearly fifty years without any change, and suddenly we get this bill of my hon. friend, which to me seems to be an unintentional reflection on members of the Government past, present or future. Ministers from time to time have usually been men of good standing in business and of high personal honour, and it has been the custom of this country and of Parliament to trust them implicitly, in the belief that they will give to the country their best service; and l think we can well trust to the honour of our ministers to give us the same faithful service in future as we have received in the past.
What my hon. friend from East Toronto (Sir Edward Kemp) is putting before you is, I understand, this:	If a gentleman under the name of John Smith, or John Smith & Company, has an enormous business it does not matter whether it is a partnership or not, he has a capital of say, one, two, or three million dollars, and although he may be dealing in every thing that the Government wants, he cannot enter into any contract with the Government because our Independence of Parliament Act prevents it. But adopting the system under which most modern business is conducted, he forms a joint stock company. Then under my hon. friend's Bill as brought in to-day that man on becoming a Minister of the Crown would have to resign as president or director of that company. When all is said and done, we want to get into Parliament men from all walks of life. It is the successful business men of the country who have arrived at an important position in the business world that a Prime Minister is anxious to bring into his Government, and it would be very hard indeed if any business man had to resign even from the directorship of the company which he has made a success. It is not in the public interest to ask him to resign from directorship or control of his company. So long as we are protected by the statute as it is, and so long as a member of Parliament who is a partner in a firm, as such cannot enter into a contract with the Government, and so long as a member who is a shareholder in a company cannot have his company take a contract for any public works, it seems to me the public are amply protected. On the whole I think it would be better to leave this matter to the good taste and good sense of present and future ministers rather than to pass special legislation to deal with it. It is certainly very
much in the public interest that a minister's conduct should be above reproach. I think in the past our ministers have been men of the highest standing, and I am sure that that standard is not likely to go down but rather will go up. For myself, I think it will be better to leave the law as it is.

This Act shall not extend to disqualify any person as a member of the House of Commons by reason of his being,-
(a) a shareholder in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement with the Government of Canada, except any company which undertakes a contract for the building of any public work.
It might be quite proper to amend the Act and cover other things, but that is a totally different matter. I would be quite willing to consider any such amendment when it does not deal with the question of a man having to resign as a director if he wants to take a Cabinet position. My contention is that it is better to leave the law as it is, and that it is not in the interests of good administration in this country to force men to resign business affiliations which they have built up during the period of a lifetime.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is said that in this discussion we need not he affected by party ideas, and, it seems to me, there can be no criticism whatever of the way in which the matter has been presented by the hon. member who gave us his reasons why the legislation he proposes should be enacted. But unfortunately I rather resent Bills of this kind, in that they are a statutory invasion of the realm of private honour and private morality. I always feel, and always have-felt, that when Parliament attempts by statute to regulate the conduct of public men or judges they are doing something which in the end does not help the public. If the public gets to believe that everything is done by statute, then there will be not so much anxiety to preserve private honour. I feel like being rather a drag on the wheels of justice when they go outside the

realms of crime and take up private matters.
In addition to that, I have an idea that it is not good to present to the public a predication of possible impropriety of conduct of gentlemen who are chosen as ministers of the Crown. The public should not have the idea spread upon the statutes that ministers of the Crown would do anything Which would interfere with their conduct of public business or their own dignity. It is true that a statute was passed a few years ago limiting the activities of * judges, but, as I recollect, it was not for the reason that judges would try cases in which they were interested, but that some judges, on account of the inadequacy of their salaries were inclined to go into business and were not giving sufficient time to their work on the bench.
It seems to me that if my hon. friend from Brome had suggested that the circumstances at the present time required this legislation, he would have made his argument much stronger, because I believe none of us know of any cases which have in any way indicated that ministers of the Crown have swerved from their duty simply because they happened to be bank or company directors.
There is another reason against this Bill, although perhaps this might be better discussed in committee. The Bill goes too far in that it makes no distinction between a large company which might affect a man's action and mind, and a small company in a man's home town which has nothing to do with the Government business at all. By passing the Bill in its present form we would to a large extent interfere with the rights of people in the country who had invested their means in companies only for the reason that they trusted the men who afterwards become Cabinet ministers. It is most unusual to find a man fit for a Cabinet position who is not a director of cone or more companies, especially companies of a local character, and the people [DOT]of the district in all probability invested their money solely for the reason that a prominent local man being president or director of the company they knew their money was safe. If by statute we do away with the right of that man to be a director, then we affect the rights of those who have invested their money. In other words, in the case of a man who becomes a Cabinet minister and is a trustee for people who have invested their money, any restrictive legislation of this kind is not in the public

For these reasons, I think that the matter might very well stand for the present, especially in view of the fact that no suggestion has been made that there is any urgent need for such legislation at this time. We are going too far, it seems to me, to think out possible improprieties when no case has presented itself to us to justify any such conclusion.
Mr. H. H. STEVENS, (Vancouver Centre) : There are only a few moments .before six o'clock, and as I should like to make a number of observations in connection with this matter, I shall say just a few words before the Houses rises.
I think it has wholly escaped the attention of the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) who introduces the resolution what the practical effect of a measure of this kind might be. There is also the question whether it would serve any really useful end. With regard to the latter point, I fail to recall at the moment, and during the short time I have had to consider it, any outstanding instance where a minister of the Crown in Canada- speaking now of all parties-has in any way flagrantly abused his position and thus given occasion for the measure which my hon. friend now brings forward. I think it is a sound principle for this House to follow to avoid legislation that is not called for. We have altogether too much legislation in this country-altogether too many artificial safeguards, if you like, or imaginary safeguards, and it is about time that we as a Parliament studied how we could avoid legislating on various subjects rather than seek out subjects to legislate upon. I submit, in the same spirit in which my hon. friend so admirably introduced the matter, that no evidence has been forthcoming in support of this kind of legislation. That is my first point, and I think it is an important one.
Another point relates to the practical side of it. Take, for instance, the cooperative associations. I have not particularly in mind my hon. friends across the way, but it is a fact that all over the country, in nearly every county throughout the provinces, there are co-operative businesses. Now, a director of one of these co-operative associations would be debarred from membership in the Government. Or take the case of a man operating a real estate, insurance and ordinary loan business, a financial brokerage business. Invariably that class of business is carried on under some corporate name, and fre-

quently two or three men may be partners and own virtually all the stock; or the business may be entirely controlled by one man. If a member of such an organization became a minister of the Crown, he could resign his directorship on the understanding with his colleagues that when he should cease to be a minister of the Crown he would come back to his old position. In that way the Bill would, I think, put a premium on subterfuge and evasion, rather than maintain what the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) very properly referred to as the high standard of honour which has characterized the public life of Canada, from before Confederation down to the present time. There are other points to which I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker; I would move the adjournment of the debate.
